doc.title: Rob Mounsey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 9, 2025

title: From pencil and paper to Sibelius and sketches
summary: He misses pencil scores; now he sketches on six staves, types into Sibelius, delivers PDFs and discards the sketches.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Has your work changed? I’m leapfrogging but I remember talking to a fellow at Eastman named Dave Rivello. I went to his house and in his music room he’s got big score pads. Yellow King score pads. He insists on writing in pencil.
And do you miss those days or how has it affected the way you work?

I do miss them a lot. Excuse me one second. I just happen to have some right here. Sturdy staff paper. Yes. The process has changed and I’m not real happy about it. It used to be always pencil and paper, finish it, fold it in half, put the title and the date on it, and send it away to somebody, to a copyist who would then write the parts out by hand. Definitely come from that old school. And nowadays I type stuff into Sibelius because people want, they just want me to deliver PDFs. So I deliver PDFs of scores and parts. Since I have to type everything into the score I can’t make myself write it out long hand in pencil anymore so for big orchestra things I generally make a six staff sketch, which is, you know, double staff woodwinds, brass and strings, and whatever other little notes I put in there. You know, sketch everything out because the most important thing is to have all of the bars, all the bar numbers, all the rehearsal letters, you know, any extra double bars to demarcate phrases between rehearsal letters, and — but you know I’m sketching out all the ideas, a lot of the voicings, especially the counterpoint, because the counterpoint’s really, really important to me. And that has to really be worked out so it really works. So that’s all in the sketch and then I type into Sibelius and I work out most of the little details as I’m typing it in, and throw the sketch away.
No, no. You have to save it.

I’m sorry, they’re gone. The sketches are gone, I have all the files, you know I have all the Sibelius files and the PDFs, so there’s no information lost. You know I can’t make myself believe that the sketches are going to be in the Smithsonian someday, like they’re gonna be, someone’s gonna care. I really doubt it.
